Large language models for question-driven chemometric analysis: Automated generation of R workflows
abstract: ABSTRACT Chemometrics has become an essential tool in analytical chemistry due to the increasing complexity and dimensionality of modern datasets. However, many researchers and students lack both the coding skills and a clear methodological roadmap required to perform a comprehensive chemometric analysis. In this work, we propose a structured, question-driven workflow comprising 17 sequential questions that guide users through a complete chemometric analysis using large language models (LLMs). The workflow includes data inspection, assessment of normality, identification of discriminative variables, unsupervised analyses by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA), and construction and validation of Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) models. The workflow was demonstrated using a previously reported lung cancer lipidomics dataset ( Sci. Transl. Med. , 14 , eabk2756, 2022) containing the concentrations of nine lipids measured in healthy controls and lung cancer patients. All analyses were performed in R using scripts generated by ChatGPT (GPT-5.5), Google Gemini (Flash-Lite), and DeepSeek (V4) in response to each analytical question. The generated scripts were executed directly in R to produce all figures and statistical analyses. The three LLMs successfully reproduced the complete exploratory chemometric workflow, whereas reproducible PLS-DA validation required explicit specification of preprocessing and cross-validation parameters. These results demonstrate that LLMs can substantially lower the technical barrier to chemometric analysis by providing methodological guidance and executable R code, making rigorous multivariate data analysis more accessible for both education and research.

DD-SIMCA coupled with LOVE variable selection for enhanced detection of corn flour adulteration with black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) using portable NIR spectroscopy
abstract: Food adulteration represents a significant challenge to ensuring authenticity, particularly in powdered matrices such as corn flour. In this study, a rapid and non-destructive methodology was developed to detect corn flour adulteration with black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) flour using portable near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy combined with DD-SIMCA modelling and LOVE variable selection. Authentic and adulterated samples were analysed at adulteration levels ranging from 1% to 20%, and spectra were acquired in the 900-1600 nm range. Spectral data were pre-processed using the Savitzky–Golay first derivative, standard normal variate (SNV), and mean centering. PCA revealed a compositional gradient associated with increasing adulteration level, although some overlap remained at the lowest concentrations. Application of the LOVE method reduced the number of variables from 212 to 92 while retaining the most informative spectral regions for model development. The DD-SIMCA model developed using the selected variables outperformed the full-spectrum model, achieving a sensitivity of 1.00 for the target class and a specificity of 1.00 in the independent external test set. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology for food authenticity assessment under the experimental conditions investigated.

abstract: The Elemental Blend Solver (EBS v9.0.2) is a browser-native application for reconstructing the elemental composition of a target compound from a massweighted blend of up to five source materials. EBS formulates the problem as constrained Non-Negative Least Squares (NNLS) and applies the Lawson–Hanson active-set algorithm to produce non-negative mixing fractions summing to unity. The software embeds a curated 73-material database spanning 20 elements in a single HTML file (∼255 KB) requiring no installation, server, or network access. Sixteen analysis tools comprise seven chart views (six quantitative plus one pedagogic Convergence Plot) and nine quantitative panel diagnostics, including Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, PCA database coverage mapping, ternary SSR contouring, exhaustive optimal blend search, and solution space exploration. A dimensionless fit index bounded (0, 1], the Global Decomposability Score (GDS), provides an instrument-independent blend-quality signal requiring no statistical tables. Validation across a 20-molecule test suite confirms exact recovery (SSR < 10−8 ) for hull-interior targets and minimum-error approximation for infeasible targets. Computational validation against published CHNS combustion data [32] confirms noise-floor elemental recovery (RMSEpp ≤ 0.050 pp, within single-σ CHN instrument noise) across seven fully-represented blend cases (p ≥ 0.860); absent-source cases are correctly identified by the χ 2 diagnostic (p < 0.001), confirming graceful degradation. Halogen mass balance constrains PVC identification to sub-0.1 pp precision. Together, these capabilities deliver a complete, validated analytical workbench accessible to any practitioner via a standard web browser. EBS is freely available under the MIT license (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19263118).

Kernel variance-constrained partial least squares for robust nonlinear regression
abstract: In high-dimensional spectroscopic analysis, traditional Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression often suffers from overfitting and sensitivity to noise, especially when $p \gg n$. While Variance Constrained PLS (VCPLS) enhances stability through regularization, it remains limited by its linear assumption. This paper proposes a novel regression framework, Kernel Variance Constrained Partial Least Squares (KVCPLS). By integrating a variance-based constraint directly into the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), KVCPLS simultaneously addresses non-linearities and suppresses unstable spectral components. Theoretically, we demonstrate that KVCPLS achieves a tighter generalization error bound compared to standard KPLS and robust PLS variants. The computational complexity is optimized to $O(n^2p + n^3 + AIn^2)$ for training, ensuring suitability for high-throughput industrial tasks. Experimental results on five benchmark datasets indicate that KVCPLS consistently outperforms PLS, KPLS, and IRPLS, achieving an average reduction in RMSEP of 12.87\%. KVCPLS provides a robust and efficient solution for complex non-linear calibration, offering a solid theoretical foundation for real-time online monitoring in demanding industrial environments.

nirs4all: Canonical, content-addressed workflows for reproducible near-infrared calibration
abstract: A published near-infrared calibration is rarely a fully reproducible one. Its reported error depends on analyst decisions about signal representation, scatter correction, replicate handling, validation design, latent-variable selection, aggregation and model family. These decisions usually survive as scripts and output files rather than as one re-executable calibration object. We present nirs4all, an open-source Python system for making that object explicit. The contribution is a computer technique for chemometric reproducibility, not a new calibration algorithm. nirs4all records preprocessing and latent-variable search as canonical workflow declarations, links predictions and fitted artefacts back to the exact fold, chain and dataset hashes that produced them, and makes validation semantics such as signal type, replicate-grouped splitting and specimen-level aggregation first-class. A controller layer lets standard Python estimators and near-infrared operators share this workflow, provenance and deployment contract. On public datasets we show deterministic representation and verifiable provenance under a pinned environment, held-out partial-least-squares reporting isolated from selection, auditable replicate policy, and bounded operational cost. This is reproducibility of the declaration and lineage; strict bitwise numerical replay still requires a pinned environment or container. nirs4all is available at https://github.com/GBeurier/nirs4all (pip install nirs4all, AGPL-3.0-or-later primary public licence).

Multivariate evaluation of the influence of soil perturbation on REE distribution and accumulation patterns in plants
abstract: The demand for Rare Earth Elements (REE) is rapidly increasing due to their widespread use in advanced technologies, making them emerging environmental contaminants. Although non-essential for plants, REE can accumulate in plant tissues and transfer through trophic levels, raising questions about how plants respond to changes in soil REE composition. This study investigates the effect of soil REE perturbation on their accumulation and distribution in Vitis vinifera L .. To this end, a full factorial (3 2 ) experimental design was implemented, combining three levels of treatment (control, low, high) with three sampling positions (soil, roots, leaves). The contribution of treatment, position, and their interaction was assessed using ANOVA–Simultaneous Component Analysis (ASCA) with permutation-based significance testing. The consistency of the inferred results was evaluated across different data processing strategies. First, inter-individual dispersion among experimental replicates was minimized through an orthogonal projection. Second, a dedicated ASCA without soil samples was performed to highlight if the significance of the position effect was driven by the artificial addition of REE. Results showed that treatment was the main driver of REE accumulation. Notably, the interaction between treatment and position explained more variance than position alone, indicating that REE distribution across compartments is modulated by soil enrichment level. The proposed approach offers a robust framework for investigating complex soil–plant interactions and supports targeted sampling strategies for field-based REE monitoring.

title: Confidence intervals for Partial Least Squares: A second-order Edgeworth expansion approach
abstract: Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression is a cornerstone of chemometric modeling, particularly for multivariate calibration where predictors (e.g., spectral channels) exhibit extreme multicollinearity. While point estimation is well-established, reliable inference in finite samples remains problematic due to the nonlinear nature of the PLS estimator. This paper introduces a novel second-order accurate confidence interval based on a bootstrap-calibrated Edgeworth expansion. Unlike first-order asymptotic methods, our approach explicitly corrects for the skewness and kurtosis inherent in PLS distributions under strong collinearity. Using an extensive Monte Carlo framework, we show that the proposed Edgeworth bootstrap method provides the most accurate coverage, especially in small samples and under strong collinearity. These findings offer practical guidance for applied researchers conducting inference in PLS regression.

title: Uniqueness in multivariate curve resolution, re-tuned
abstract: There are many misunderstandings about the term and interpretation of uniqueness in multivariate curve resolution tasks. In CAC2026 Tarragona, it turned out that even mathematicians do not properly construe Manne’s theorems. So we decided to provide this re-tuned summary, using several original quotes, their explanations, and newly created illustrative figures to get the points across. This contribution then explicitly offers the following: (i) a unified interpretation of Manne’s conditions, DBU, GRU, minimal constrained duality, and particular-solution-based criteria; (ii) newly constructed visual illustrations, including a counterexample; and (iii) a practical workflow for diagnosing uniqueness in nonnegative bilinear MCR.

title: Instrument-shift-informed source-domain augmentation for calibration transfer in near-infrared spectroscopy
Chemometrics Web App: Synthetic Sampling
abstract: ABSTRACT This work reports the release and usability of the Chemometrics Web App: Synthetic Sampling (CWA: SS), an open-source application developed in the R environment with the Shiny package to address class imbalance in analytical and chemometric datasets. By leveraging the reticulate package, CWA: SS integrates Python’s imbalanced-learn library into a unified graphical user interface made on the basis of Shiny package on posit platform, offering 16 sampling algorithms, including oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid methods. A fundamental contribution of this application is the implementation of a systematized strategy to evaluate the efficiency and quality of synthetic sampling before the predictive modeling phase. This diagnostic module incorporates multivariate tools, such as Generalized Procrustes Analysis, PERMANOVA, Hotelling T 2 , and spectral profile comparisons, to ensure that synthetic data preserve original chemical and structural relationships without introducing artifacts or bias to the synthetic data. The application’s performance was validated through two distinct scenarios: a multiclass QSAR dataset, and a portable NIR spectral dataset (900–1700 nm) used to identify the integrity of Jatobá fruit. The results demonstrate that CWA: SS effectively handles multiclass problems and maintains the integrity of complex spectral profiles. The software is accessible via standalone executable, or cloud-based hosting through the LTAP website ( https://www.ltapuerj.com.br ), providing a flexible and user-friendly tool for both laboratory and field-based research without the need for programming expertise.

title: Cross-study shift defines the reliability limits of FTIR polymer classification
abstract: Automated Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) classifiers for microplastics are often evaluated by randomly splitting spectra pooled from several studies, although deployment requires transfer to new sources. We harmonized 4,783 labelled spectra from four independent studies and compared a study-mixed random split with leave-one-study-out (LOSO) evaluation. We then examined task composition, source-associated structure, nested deep and domain-oriented models, external reference-library pooling, and selective prediction on locked domains. XGBoost achieved random-split macro-F1 of 0.972 but equal-study present-class LOSO macro-F1 of 0.672. The gap was class- and source-dependent: PE/PP transfer remained strong, whereas adding PET and PS reopened most of the shared-fold deficit despite adequate class support. Polymer class dominated the global geometry of the harmonized data, yet source study remained highly predictable, including within PE and PP. Position-aware convolutional, self-supervised and domain-adversarial configurations did not consistently outperform XGBoost, and external libraries produced non-monotonic effects, indicating that directional compatibility mattered more than library size. A maximum-probability threshold selected only from inner study holdouts identified lower-risk subsets on locked De Frond and Open Specy domains, although coverage was domain-dependent. These results support a practical trust framework for multi-source FTIR classification: validate by study, report fold- and support-aware metrics, screen external libraries for compatibility, and defer spectra outside the model's reliable operating region.

Robust preprocessing and peak extraction method for machine learning-based classification of surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) provides sensitive molecular detection, but spectra acquired from heterogeneous substrates can span logarithmic intensity ranges. This nuisance variation can dominate distances and fitted decision functions even when peak locations remain informative. We present Blurred Laplacian Peak Extraction (BLaPE), a scale-selective preprocessing transform that smooths a spectrum at an expected peak-width scale, computes its rectified negative Laplacian, and normalizes the curvature response by signal magnitude. The resulting features encode peak presence within the [0, 1] range. We evaluated the method using 17,875 SERS spectra from 376 dyed and aged organic dye specimens prepared across substrate, dye, mordant, and aging factors. For dye identification, BLaPE reduced the classification error from 26.31 to 8.38% for cosine k-nearest neighbors and from 24.28 to 9.09% for random forest. Improvements were smaller for higher-capacity neural networks, and conventional scaling remained comparable or better for some of these models. An independent public Raman benchmark reproduced this model-capacity-dependent pattern, with the largest gains for instance-based and classical classifiers. BLaPE therefore provides an interpretable peak-centered representation for classification problems in which large spectral intensity variation would otherwise dominate the input.

IC-DA chemometric tool coupled to MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for organic spices and herbs evaluation
abstract: The consumer demand for healthy food contributes to the growth of organic food consumption, which in turn increases the price of this type of food. Among the organic products, spices and herbs stand out for their characteristic flavor and bioactive compounds. Considering the lack of applications of the analytical technique based on Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS) in the evaluation of organic foods, as well as the absence of Independent Components Discriminant Analysis (IC-DA) chemometric application in organic food discrimination, this work aims to propose a method for the discrimination of organic and non-organic cinnamon, mint, oregano, and rosemary using MALDI-TOF-MS coupled with IC-DA. The method proved effective in differentiating between organic and conventional spices, advancing our understanding of the classes of compounds that distinguish these two farming practices. The results highlight the potential of this innovative approach for rapid screening and evaluation of organic food through high-throughput analysis, with minimal sample preparation and relatively low per-sample costs, supporting its suitability for routine applications in organic food authentication.

abstract: Portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) spectroscopy enables precise, non-destructive elemental characterization of cultural heritage materials, yet traditional point-based measurements inherently overlook the spatial and chromatic variability of the pictorial application. To address this limitation, a data-driven chemometric pipeline was developed to integrate high-dimensional compositional data (pXRF) with chromatic and textural descriptors derived from multidimensional fractal analysis (FD-RGB and FD-Gray). Using a historical copy of Raphael's “The Transfiguration” as a comprehensive case study, 165 localized XRF elemental profiles were statistically associated with fractal descriptors extracted from high-resolution digital patches. This single-painting case study is framed as a proof of concept, and the resulting pigment-texture relationships are interpreted as preliminary and case-dependent rather than as universal thresholds. Rank-based correlation analysis, Kruskal-Wallis tests, Dunn post-hoc comparisons with Benjamini–Hochberg control across contrasts, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) were applied to evaluate the multivariate behavior of specific major chemical families. The integrated analysis demonstrates a directional mathematical decoupling of luminance-based texture from chromatic complexity. Results indicate that luminance variations (quantified via FD-Gray) show minimal dependence on the localized chemical palette, while multiscale chromatic variance (FD-RGB) effectively discriminates between opaque and multilayered applications (|ρ| ≈ 0.17-0.22; several remained significant under within-descriptor false-discovery-rate control). Specifically, pigments defining high-hiding matrices (based on Pb, Sn) reduce the chromatic complexity (FD-RGB), whereas pigments historically associated with chiaroscuro and translucent glazes (based on Hg, Mn, Ca) markedly increase this fractal complexity. In a dominance-based variance analysis, FD-RGB differed across groups ( p = 0.018; η 2 = 0.222), while Dunn pairwise differences were nominal at the unadjusted level. PCA of the standardized matrix (18 elemental variables + FD-RGB/FD-Gray) showed that PC1 (33.03%) aligns with an opacity-translucency continuum driven by Pb, Ba, As, Cd, and Sb, opposed to FD-RGB, whereas PC2 (11.77%) separates cool (based on Co, Ni, and Cu) from warm/shadow domains (based on Ca, Mn, Fe, and Hg) with FD-RGB loading negatively. This data-driven framework transforms raw chemical data into objective art-technical knowledge, demonstrating its capacity to characterize painterly execution beyond pigment concentration, and offering a robust new computational tool for Heritage Science.
